sec:subgraphs.section: Subgraphs Based on Session Referrer URL

nodes.name: Local Ranking Problem (LRP)
nodes.statement: This practical issue raises the problem of how well one can estimate the actual centrality value of a node by knowing only a local portion of the graph. This is known as the \textit{Local Ranking Problem} (LRP)~\cite{Chen2004}.
nodes.statement_short: Estimate the centrality (PageRank) value of a node knowing only a local portion of the graph.

nodes.name: Bressan-Pretto impossibility of efficient local ranking
nodes.statement: Bressan and Pretto~\cite{Bressan2011} proved that, in the general case, an efficient local ranking algorithm does not exist, and in order to compute a {\it correct} ranking it is necessary to visit at least a number of nodes linear in the size of the input graph.
conclusions: an efficient local ranking algorithm does not exist
in order to compute a {\it correct} ranking it is necessary to visit at least a number of nodes linear in the size of the input graph
nodes.statement_short: In general no efficient local ranking algorithm exists: a correct ranking requires visiting a linear number of nodes.

nodes.name: ReferrerGraph
nodes.statement: They introduced the concept of \textit{ReferrerGraph}, which is a \textit{BrowseGraph}\ built with sessions that are generated by the same referrer domain.
differentia: built with sessions that are generated by the same referrer domain

nodes.name: BrowseGraph
nodes.statement:
The \textit{BrowseGraph}\ is a graph whose nodes are web pages, and whose edges are the
browsing transitions made by the users.
nodes.origin_citation: Liu et al. 2008; Trevisiol et al. 2012, 2014
differentia:
whose edges are the
browsing transitions made by the users

nodes.name: Session splitting rule
nodes.statement:
We split the activity of a single user, taking the \textit{BCookie} as an
identifier, into different sessions when either of these two conditions holds:
\begin{itemize}
  \item {\bf Timeout:} the inactivity between two pageviews is longer than $25$ minutes.
  \item {\bf External URL:} if a user leaves the news platform and returns from an external domain, the current session ends even if previous visits are within the 25 minute threshold.
nodes.statement_short: A user's pageviews are split into sessions on a 25-minute inactivity timeout or on return from an external domain.

nodes.name: Referrer-based subgraph
nodes.statement: For each source domain we extract a subgraph from the overall \textit{BrowseGraph}, by considering only the browsing sessions whose initial {\textit Referrer URL} matches that domain. For example, if a user clicks on a link referring to our network that has been posted on Twitter, her {\textit Referrer URL} will be the Twitter page where she found the link. Next, we consider all the following pageviews belonging to the same session of the user, as being a part of the {\it twitter-subgraph}, given that all of them have been reached through Twitter.
nodes.section: 3.2 Subgraphs Based on Session Referrer URL
nodes.statement_short: The subgraph of a source domain consists of all browsing sessions whose initial Referrer URL matches that domain.

nodes.name: Edge weight
nodes.statement: The \textit{Weight} accounts for the number of times a user has navigated from the source page to the destination page.
nodes.section: 3.2 Subgraphs Based on Session Referrer URL

nodes.name: Referrer subgraphs yield dissimilar PageRank rankings
nodes.statement:
Interestingly, most of the similarity values tend to be very low (<0.3),
confirming the hypothesis that the user's interests are tightly related to the
domain where they come from. Some of these similarities, however, are
considerably higher, remarkably the ones between the three subgraphs that are
originated from search engines traffic, \emph{i.e.}, Bing, Google and Yahoo, which yield
the most similar rankings of pages (>0.5).
conclusions: most of the similarity values tend to be very low (<0.3)

the ones between the three subgraphs that are
originated from search engines traffic, \emph{i.e.}, Bing, Google and Yahoo, which yield
the most similar rankings of pages (>0.5)
nodes.statement_short: Kendall's tau between PageRank rankings of referrer subgraphs is mostly below 0.3, except among search-engine subgraphs (>0.5).

nodes.name: Referrer identification from a random surfer trace
nodes.statement:
Therefore, we consider the following scenario: a content provider is observing a user
surfing the pages of its web service, but it is unaware of the user's referrer URL. 
In terms of our experimental dataset, this scenario maps into the problem of observing a browsing trace left by a random surfer on one of the referrer-based subgraphs and having to identify which graph it is.
nodes.statement_short: Given a browsing trace on one of the referrer subgraphs, identify which subgraph generated it.

nodes.name: RandomSurfer
nodes.statement_short: Simulate a damped random walk on $G_k$ and accumulate, for every subgraph $G_i$, the log-probability of the observed trace under a PageRank-style walk on $G_i$.

nodes.name: Maximum log-likelihood referrer identification
nodes.statement:
Formally, observing the sequence of the surfer's visited nodes $\mathbf{x}=(x_1, x_2, \dots,
x_s)$ and computing the probability $p_i(\mathbf{x})$ that the surfer has gone
through them given that it is surfing $G_i$, we need to deduce what is
$G_i$ (\emph{e.g.}, by maximum log-likelihood). With this goal in mind, we sort the indices of
the subgraphs $i_1,i_2,\dots$ so that $p_{i_1}(\mathbf{x})\geq
p_{i_2}(\mathbf{x}) \geq \dots$ and stop as soon as the gap between $\log
p_{i_1}(\mathbf{x})$ and $\log p_{i_2}(\mathbf{x})$ is large enough (\emph{e.g.}, $\log
p_{i_1}(\mathbf{x})-\log p_{i_2}(\mathbf{x}) \geq \log 2$), 
with a maximum of $20$ steps that we consider as a representation of a long user session.
input:
the sequence of the surfer's visited nodes $\mathbf{x}=(x_1, x_2, \dots,
x_s)$
nodes.statement_short: Rank subgraphs by the likelihood of the observed trace and stop once the top log-likelihood exceeds the runner-up by $\log 2$ (max 20 steps).

nodes.statement:

through them given that it is surfing $G_i$
nodes.statement_short: Compute the probability of the trace under each subgraph.

p_{i_2}(\mathbf{x}) \geq \dots$

p_{i_1}(\mathbf{x})-\log p_{i_2}(\mathbf{x}) \geq \log 2$), 
with a maximum of $20$ steps that we consider as a representation of a long user session.
nodes.statement_short: Stop when the log-likelihood gap is at least $\log 2$, or after 20 steps.

nodes.name: Damping factor $\alpha$
nodes.statement:
Recall that $\alpha$ is the balancing parameter that determines
the probability of following in the random walk, instead of teleporting.

nodes.name: Referrer recognizable at the first step
nodes.statement: Almost all the referrer domains are recognizable at the first step.
conclusions: Almost all the referrer domains are recognizable at the first step.

nodes.name: Growing Rings expansion
input: a graph $H$ which is a subgraph of the full graph $G$
nodes.statement_short: BFS-style expansion: each ring adds all out-neighbours of the current ring and takes the induced subgraph.

nodes.name: Initialize ring
nodes.statement: $H_0 \longleftarrow H$;
nodes.statement_short: Start from the local subgraph.

nodes.name: Add out-neighbours
nodes.statement: $V_{H_{k+1}} \longleftarrow \{\Gamma_{out}(V_{H_k}) \cup V_{H_k}\}$, with $V_x$ being the set of vertices of a graph, and $\Gamma$ being the vertex neighborhood function;
nodes.statement_short: Next vertex set: current vertices plus their out-neighbours.

nodes.name: Induce edges
nodes.statement: $E_{H_{k+1}} \longleftarrow \{(v_1, v_2) | v_1 \in V_{H_{k+1}} \wedge v_2 \in V_{H_{k+1}} \}$, with $E_x$ being the set of edges of a graph.
nodes.statement_short: Take all edges among the new vertex set.

nodes.name: Rings
nodes.statement:
We refer to the various steps of this
expansion as \textit{``rings''}, where the ring $H_0$ is the initial subgraph
and subsequent rings are obtained by adding all the outgoing arcs that depart
from the nodes in the current ring and end in nodes that are not in the ring.
nodes.statement_short: The successive graphs of the Growing Rings expansion, starting from $H_0$.

nodes.name: Rings beyond $H_0$ are induced subgraphs
nodes.statement:
Observe that, depending on how it is built, $H_0$ may not be
an induced subgraph of $G$, but $H_1, \cdots, H_n$ are always induced subgraphs, by
definition of the expansion algorithm.
conclusions:
$H_0$ may not be
an induced subgraph of $G$

nodes.name: Referrer-based (RB) initial subgraphs
nodes.statement: \textbf{Referrer-based (RB)}. The seven browsing subgraphs built by referrer URL: Facebook, Twitter, Reddit, Homepage, Yahoo, Google and Bing;

nodes.name: Same size referrer-based (SRB) initial subgraphs
nodes.statement: \textbf{Same size referrer-based (SRB)}. To measure how much the different sizes of the graphs impact on the observed behavior, we fix a number of nodes and extract a portion of each subgraph in order to obtain exactly the same size for all networks. The selection is performed with several attempts of BFS expansion, starting from a random node in each graph, until the resulting graphs have very similar size ($\pm 9.4\%$): other ways of selecting subgraphs would end up with disconnected samples, which of course would void the purpose of this experiment. With this procedure instead, we are able to compare the graphs on equal grounds and at the same time control for the effect of size (about $3K$ nodes and $20K$ edges).
nodes.statement_short: Equal-size (about 3K nodes) portions of each referrer subgraph obtained by BFS from a random node.

nodes.name: Random (R) initial subgraphs
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Random (R)}. To check whether the observed behavior has to do with the user behavior underlying the graph under examination (\textit{e.g.}, the particular structure of the graph determined by the sessions of users coming from Twitter), we take a set of seven \textit{random} graphs each of them reflecting the size of each of the referrer-based subgraphs. 
Thus, we can explore the behavior of browsing graphs, which preserve the size of the graphs originated by specific types of users, but that are ``artificial'' in the sense that destroy any connection with the behavior connected to a particular user class. To make sure that the size is the same, we start from a BFS exploration and we prune the last level to match exactly the size we need.
nodes.statement_short: Seven BFS-sampled random subgraphs of the full graph, each matching the size of one referrer subgraph.

nodes.name: Fast Growing Rings convergence for RB
nodes.statement:
The convergence happens relatively quickly,
as the value $\tau$ approaches $1$ in the first $3$ iterations. The curves
related to different subgraphs are shifted with respect to each other,
apparently mainly due to their different size, the biggest networks starting
from higher $\tau$ values and converging faster than the smaller ones.
conclusions:
The convergence happens relatively quickly,
as the value $\tau$ approaches $1$ in the first $3$ iterations.
nodes.statement_short: On RB subgraphs Kendall's tau to global PageRank approaches 1 within 3 rings; larger graphs start higher and converge faster.

nodes.name: Structural differences persist at equal size
nodes.statement: Even if the curves resulted to be more flattened (confirming that the initial size has indeed a role in the convergence), we still observe noticeable differences between the curves for the first two expansion levels. This means that different subgraphs are substantially different from one another in terms of their structure: even after forcing them to have the same size, the convergence rates observed on the different graphs varies. At the first iteration, for instance, all the subgraphs in \textbf{SRB}  have Kendall's $\tau$ between $0.3$ and $0.5$, whereas the ones in \textbf{RB} are between $0.4$ and $0.6$.
nodes.statement_short: Even at equal size (SRB) convergence rates differ across subgraphs, showing structural differences.

nodes.name: Random subgraphs converge more slowly
nodes.statement: Results, displayed in Figure~\ref{fig:growinrings} (right), show that convergence in this case is much slower and the difference between the curves is less prominent.

nodes.name: Growing Rings with selection of top-PageRank nodes
nodes.statement:
More formally, considering $H_k$ as the subgraph at iteration $k$ and $V_{H_k}$
its set of nodes, we select all the external nodes in $Y = \{V_G \backslash V_{H_k}\}$,
which are connected through outgoing arcs from the nodes in $V_{H_k}$.
We then compute the PageRank values on the subgraph $H_k$ extended with the
nodes $Y$ and obtain a ranked list of nodes. Among all the nodes in $Y$ we
select the top $n\%$ with largest PageRank value, and only those ones will be
added to $H_k$ in order to build $H_{k+1}$ and advance to the next iteration.

nodes.statement_short: Partial ring expansion: among the out-neighbours of $H_k$, add only the top $n\%$ by PageRank on the extended graph.

nodes.name: Few top-PageRank nodes converge faster initially
nodes.statement:
Remarkably,
the figure highlights how expanding the graph by adding fewer nodes, although
the most representative ones, leads to PageRank values that are closer to the
\emph{global} ones in the first iterations.
nodes.section: 5.2 Growing Rings with Selection of Nodes
nodes.statement_short: Adding only the top-PageRank neighbours gives PageRank closer to the global one in the first iterations.

nodes.name: Full expansion converges closer to 1 in the long run
nodes.statement:
Contrarily, in the long run, expansions that include the highest number of nodes
present convergence values closer to $1$.

nodes.name: Prediction of the local-global Kendall $\tau$
nodes.statement: We address the problem of predicting the Kendall's $\tau$ between the local and the global PageRank, only considering information available on the local graph such as topological features.

nodes.name: Jackknife regression of Kendall $\tau$ from structural features
nodes.statement:
Starting from the
seven subgraphs in the dataset, we build a training set using the jackknife
approach, by removing nodes in bulks ($1\%$, $5\%$, $10\%$, $20\%$) and
computing the $\tau$ value between the full subgraph and their reduced versions.
Then, for each instance in the training set we compute $62$ structural graph
metrics~\cite{wasserman94social,Barrat2008} belonging to the following
categories:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Size and connectivity (S)}. Statistics on the size and basic wiring
properties, such as number of nodes and edges, graph density, reciprocity,
number of connected components, relative size of the biggest component.
\item \textbf{Assortativity (A)}. The tendency of node with a certain degree, to be
linked with nodes with similar degree. We computed different combinations that
take into account the in/out/full degree of the target node vs. the in/out/full
degree of the nodes that are connected with it.
\item \textbf{Degree (D)}. Statistics (average, median, standard deviation, \emph{etc.}) on
the degree distribution of nodes.
\item \textbf{Weighted degree (W)}. Same as \textbf{degree}, but considering the
weight on edges, which usually referred as node strength. As the edges are the
transitions made by the users during the navigation, the weight stand for the
number of times the users have navigated the transition.
\item \textbf{Local Pagerank (P)}. Statistics on the distribution of the PageRank
values computed on the local graph.
\item \textbf{Closeness centralization (C)}. Statistics on the distances (number of
hops), which separate a node to the others in the graph, in the spirit of the
closeness centralization~\cite{wasserman94social}.
\end{itemize}
We employed different regression algorithms, although we report the performance
using random forests~\cite{Breiman:2001:RF:570181.570182}, which performed
better in this scenario than other approaches like support vector
regression~\cite{Smola03atutorial}. We computed the mean square error (MSE)
across all examples in all sampled subgraphs. 
The random forest regression has been computed over a five-fold cross validation averaged over $10$ iterations.
input:
the
seven subgraphs in the dataset
nodes.statement_short: Build a jackknife training set by removing node bulks, compute 62 structural metrics per sample, and regress Kendall's tau with random forests under cross-validation.

nodes.name: Jackknife sampling
nodes.statement:
Starting from the
seven subgraphs in the dataset, we build a training set using the jackknife
approach, by removing nodes in bulks ($1\%$, $5\%$, $10\%$, $20\%$) and
computing the $\tau$ value between the full subgraph and their reduced versions.
nodes.statement_short: Remove 1-20% of nodes in bulk and compute tau between the full subgraph and each reduced version.

nodes.name: Compute structural features
nodes.statement:
Then, for each instance in the training set we compute $62$ structural graph
metrics~\cite{wasserman94social,Barrat2008} belonging to the following
categories:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Size and connectivity (S)}. Statistics on the size and basic wiring
properties, such as number of nodes and edges, graph density, reciprocity,
number of connected components, relative size of the biggest component.
\item \textbf{Assortativity (A)}. The tendency of node with a certain degree, to be
linked with nodes with similar degree. We computed different combinations that
take into account the in/out/full degree of the target node vs. the in/out/full
degree of the nodes that are connected with it.
\item \textbf{Degree (D)}. Statistics (average, median, standard deviation, \emph{etc.}) on
the degree distribution of nodes.
\item \textbf{Weighted degree (W)}. Same as \textbf{degree}, but considering the
weight on edges, which usually referred as node strength. As the edges are the
transitions made by the users during the navigation, the weight stand for the
number of times the users have navigated the transition.
\item \textbf{Local Pagerank (P)}. Statistics on the distribution of the PageRank
values computed on the local graph.
\item \textbf{Closeness centralization (C)}. Statistics on the distances (number of
hops), which separate a node to the others in the graph, in the spirit of the
closeness centralization~\cite{wasserman94social}.
nodes.statement_short: Compute 62 structural metrics in six categories for each sample.

nodes.name: Random forest regression
nodes.statement:
We employed different regression algorithms, although we report the performance
using random forests~\cite{Breiman:2001:RF:570181.570182}, which performed
better in this scenario than other approaches like support vector
regression~\cite{Smola03atutorial}. We computed the mean square error (MSE)
across all examples in all sampled subgraphs. 
The random forest regression has been computed over a five-fold cross validation averaged over $10$ iterations.
nodes.statement_short: Fit random forest regression, evaluated by MSE under 5-fold cross-validation over 10 repetitions.

nodes.name: Weighted degree (W) features
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Weighted degree (W)}. Same as \textbf{degree}, but considering the
weight on edges, which usually referred as node strength. As the edges are the
transitions made by the users during the navigation, the weight stand for the
number of times the users have navigated the transition.
nodes.statement_short: Degree statistics using edge weights (node strength), the weights being transition counts.

nodes.name: Low cross-validated MSE
nodes.statement: The mean square residuals that we obtained is very low, around $2.4\cdot10^{-6}$.

nodes.name: Weighted degree is the most predictive feature class
nodes.statement:
The most predictive feature category is the \emph{weighted degree}, which yields a performance that is better (or comparable) than the model
using all the features. The \emph{assortativity} features instead, seem to be the ones that have the less predictive power on their own.
nodes.statement_short: Weighted-degree features predict tau as well as or better than all features; assortativity features are least predictive.

nodes.name: Predicted ranking of subgraphs by $\tau$
nodes.statement:
However, the model was able to rank the seven different subgraphs
by their Kendall's $\tau$ almost perfectly. When using all the features the
Spearman's correlation coefficient between the true order and the predicted one
is 0.85 (high correlation), and when we used the most predictive features
(weighted degree) the correlation was as high as 0.80 (moderate high
correlation). Overall, the final rankings are just one swap away (Kendall's
$\tau$ is over 0.70 in this case).
nodes.statement_short: The learned model ranks the seven subgraphs by tau almost perfectly (Spearman 0.85 with all features, 0.80 with weighted degree).
